title: Many Nichiren communities
hook: Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others differ in important ways; each speaks for itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gohonzon, the written mandala with the title down the center. Your line was the scroll. What did the thing on your wall put at its center? Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

Ask a handful of Nichiren Buddhists who Nichiren was, which scroll matters most, and who keeps the teaching, and the answers will not all match. Each one will be sincere. Each will come with reasons, and with a history of its own. A fair listener's first job is a plain one: let each answer finish before reaching for a verdict. That is today's lesson, and it closes a week spent among Japan's temple schools, from Tendai's mountain to Shingon's mandalas to the chanted title. Today: many Nichiren communities.
screen: `THE ANSWERS DON'T ALL MATCH.` → `LET EACH ONE FINISH.` → `A WEEK IN JAPAN'S SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Here are three, each as it describes itself, and none ranked. First, Nichiren Shu. It sees itself as carrying on the temple lineages of Nichiren's disciples. It honors Nichiren as a great teacher and bodhisattva sent to spread the Lotus Sutra, and it places Shakyamuni, the eternal Buddha of the Lotus Sutra, at the center of devotion. Its temples may hold statues as well as scrolls, and its members often chant namu myoho renge kyo. Second, Nichiren Shoshu. It traces its line through Nikko, one of Nichiren's senior disciples, to a head temple at the foot of Mount Fuji called Taiseki-ji. It teaches that Nichiren himself is the true Buddha for this age, and it reveres one great scroll kept at the head temple as the heart of its faith. Its priests confer the gohonzon on members. Third, Soka Gakkai. It began in Japan as a society of lay educators connected to Nichiren Shoshu. The two later parted ways, and the separation still matters to both. Soka Gakkai now describes itself as a lay Buddhist movement, with members far beyond Japan, built on chanting, study and small discussion meetings in members' homes, and on work for peace, culture and education. And there are others: Rissho Kosei-kai, Reiyukai, and the monks of Nipponzan Myohoji, who walk beating drums and build peace pagodas. Each is a sangha, a community, and each claims to be faithful to Nichiren. They differ on who he was, on which scroll is true, and on whether priests or laypeople carry the teaching. Those are not small questions. That is exactly why each deserves to be heard in its own voice, not through a rival's summary, and not through ours.
screen: `NICHIREN SHU: THE TEMPLE LINEAGES.` · `NICHIREN SHOSHU: THE HEAD TEMPLE.` · `SOKA GAKKAI: A LAY MOVEMENT.` · `OTHERS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `EACH SPEAKS FOR ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Choose one community from today, whichever stayed with you. Say its name quietly. Recall one thing it says about itself, in its own words, not in anyone else's. Hold that sentence for a few breaths without adding a but. Then turn it around: think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a faith, a town, and the first sentence you would want a stranger to hear about it. Sit with both sentences side by side. Later today, if you're curious, read a page that community wrote about itself. The bell holds the time.
Many Nichiren communities. Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others: one chant, one sutra, and real differences, each explained in its own voice. Today's word.
Your line: each speaks for itself. Today, when someone describes a group, ask once, quietly, how that group would describe itself. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists belong to several communities, among them Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, which share the Lotus Sutra and the chanted title but differ on Nichiren's role, the gohonzon and the place of priests and laypeople.

fork.setup: a friend asks you what one of these communities believes. what do you reach for first?
options: what its rivals say about it.
fork.reveal: today's way: start with the community's own words. each speaks for itself, and the differences are real enough to deserve that.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali sangha, the community: every Nichiren group is a sangha, each with its own voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nichiren Buddhism is one organization.
what it means: it is many communities sharing the Lotus Sutra and the title, differing on Nichiren's role, the scroll, and priests and laypeople.
what a scholar hears: lineages traced through different disciples, Nikko's line to Taiseki-ji among them, and a lay movement that parted from the priesthood.

notes: Please have each community's description checked against its own materials (Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai); the script aims to state each view without ranking.
Nichiren Shu: 'great teacher and bodhisattva' (often identified with Bodhisattva Superior Practices / Jogyo) and Shakyamuni as the eternal Buddha at the center: confirm.
Nichiren Shoshu: Nikko lineage, Taiseki-ji, Nichiren as True Buddha, the Dai-Gohonzon, priests conferring gohonzon: confirm.

Soka Gakkai: origin among lay educators (Makiguchi, Toda) linked to Nichiren Shoshu, later separation (deliberately undated), now issuing its own gohonzon (not stated in voice): confirm the neutral phrasing 'parted ways'.
Rissho Kosei-kai, Reiyukai, Nipponzan Myohoji listed as 'others'; confirm all three identify with the Nichiren / Lotus Sutra stream.
Week-end look back names Tendai, Shingon, the mandalas and the title (days 1338–1343); those days' scripts were not on disk when this was written.
